nodes.title: Artinian coefficients and small extensions
nodes.statement: Fix a complete Noetherian local coefficient ring Λ with a specified residue field k. Art_Λ has Artinian local Λ-algebras A, a chosen Λ-compatible A/m_A ≅ k, and local Λ-maps inducing identity on k. A small extension is a surjection B→A with a nonzero principal kernel annihilated by m_B. An elementary extension only requires m_B ker=0 and permits any finite k-dimension, including zero. A square-zero extension has kernel I with I²=0, a weaker condition.
hypotheses: Fix a complete Noetherian local coefficient ring Λ with a specified residue field k.
proofSteps: Use the existing local/Artinian ring structures with a specified residue identification. Restrict morphisms; identity and composition preserve the residue identification.
Identify an elementary kernel as a finite k-vector space. In the nonzero principal case its dimension is exactly one.
acceptance: k[ε]/ε²→k is small, with kernel kε.
k[x,y]/(x,y)²→k is elementary and square-zero, but not small.
k[t]/t⁴→k[t]/t² has square-zero kernel but m_B ker ≠0.
The identity of k has zero kernel and is not small.

nodes.title: Complete local coefficients
nodes.statement: CNL_Λ consists of complete separated Noetherian local Λ-algebras with specified residue k; morphisms are continuous local Λ-maps inducing identity on k. The topology is m-adic. No finite residue-field assumption is built into CNL_Λ; compactness through finite underlying quotients later adds it explicitly. Every object defines a compatible tower A/m_A^n, n≥1.
hypotheses: CNL_Λ consists of complete separated Noetherian local Λ-algebras with specified residue k; morphisms are continuous local Λ-maps inducing identity on k.
proofSteps: Restrict rings and maps by completeness and Noetherianity, using existing adic completion.
Identify maps with compatible quotient maps; continuity follows from locality for the m-adic topologies.

nodes.title: Cohen structure and compatible coefficients
nodes.statement: Every complete Noetherian local A is a quotient of a complete regular local Q with the same residue field. In equal characteristic Q=k[[x_1,…,x_e]] after choosing a coefficient field. For perfect residue k and mixed characteristic, an unramified regular local A of dimension d is W(k)[[x_1,…,x_{d−1}]]. A ramified regular A has A≅W(k)[[x_1,…,x_d]]/(p−f), f in (p,x_1,…,x_d)^2, with p nonzero in the quotient and p−f a nonzerodivisor in the regular ambient ring. For imperfect k use a Cohen ring, not W(k). A separable residue extension admits compatible choices of coefficient maps; no uniqueness is asserted.
hypotheses: Every complete Noetherian local A is a quotient of a complete regular local Q with the same residue field.
proofSteps: Construct a coefficient ring/field and lift a finite cotangent basis. Surjectivity of formal evaluation gives the presentation.

For a separable extension lift the coefficient embedding through the Cohen rings, then lift the remaining parameters. For imperfect residue fields retain Cohen rings instead of substituting Witt vectors.

nodes.title: Prorepresentability and automorphisms
nodes.statement: In the classical case F is prorepresentable iff H1–H4 hold. More generally a set-valued deformation functor preserving all fibre products with a surjective leg is prorepresentable iff T_F is finite and Der_Λ(k,k)→T_F is injective. For a groupoid-valued deformation category satisfying the Rim–Schlessinger fibre-product equivalence, its isomorphism-class functor preserves these fibre products iff automorphisms lift along every small extension.

proofSteps: H4 upgrades a smooth tangent-isomorphism map from a hull to a bijection by induction on length: each nonempty lifting fibre is a tangent torsor.

nodes.title: Complete obstruction theories
nodes.statement: A complete linear obstruction theory for F assigns a finite k-vector space V and, functorially for elementary extensions B→A with kernel I and x∈F(A), an obstruction o(x,B)∈V⊗_k I whose vanishing is equivalent to existence of a lift. nodes.title: Canonical type along parameters and power series
nodes.statement: For CM local A with K_A and an A-regular parameter list f of length dim A, μ_A(K_A)=dim_k Soc(A/(f)). Adjoining formal variables preserves this type. For complete local CM O-algebra B and complete local CI O-algebra C, B⊗̂_O C is CM with the same type as B when B or C is O-flat; under these hypotheses the defining regular sequence remains regular after base change. For a finite flat local O-order A, finite transitivity gives K_A≅Hom_O(A,O); A is Gorenstein iff this dual is free of rank one over A. For finite group rings, use L6’s coefficient-of-identity pairing Hom_O(O[G],O)≅O[G]. General finite-order duality is not claimed to exist in L6.
hypotheses: For CM local A with K_A and an A-regular parameter list f of length dim A, μ_A(K_A)=dim_k Soc(A/(f)).
proofSteps: Reduce K along regular parameters and use Artinian Matlis duality to identify its residue generators with the dual socle.
For the tensor product use Tor independence from O-flatness to preserve the Koszul resolution. Parameters and their reductions then identify canonical modules and type.

nodes.title: Abelian p-group rings are complete intersections
nodes.statement: For O a complete DVR of residue characteristic p and Δ=∏_{i=1}^r Z/p^{n_i}, O[Δ]≅O[[T_1,…,T_r]]/((1+T_i)^{p^{n_i}}−1)_i is finite free over O and a local CI of dimension one. For a complete local CM O-algebra B, B[Δ] is CM of the same canonical type as B. The CI assertion is restricted to finite abelian Δ, while balanced-module theory later permits arbitrary finite p-groups.
hypotheses: For O a complete DVR of residue characteristic p and Δ=∏_{i=1}^r Z/p^{n_i}, O[Δ]≅O[[T_1,…,T_r]]/((1+T_i)^{p^{n_i}}−1)_i is finite free over O and a local CI of dimension one.

Finite p-group augmentation over k makes the group algebra local; identify completion with the finite ring, then apply type preservation.

nodes.title: Trace ideals and free summands
nodes.statement: For a finite module M over commutative A define tr_A(M) as the ideal generated by {φ(m):m∈M, φ∈Hom_A(M,A)}. Over a local A, tr_A(M)=A iff M has a direct summand isomorphic to A. Define the evaluation M⊗_A Hom_A(M,A)→A, whose image is the trace ideal; no perfectness is assumed.
hypotheses: For a finite module M over commutative A define tr_A(M) as the ideal generated by {φ(m):m∈M, φ∈Hom_A(M,A)}.
proofSteps: Use existing linear maps, tensor product and ideal span of evaluation values.
If the trace contains a unit, one evaluation is a unit by locality; rescale its functional and split the resulting map A→M. The converse uses projection onto a free summand.
acceptance: A^r for r≥1 has trace A.
Over a domain A, A/(a) with a≠0 has trace zero.
For A=k[t]/t², tr_A(k)=(t), a proper nonzero ideal.

nodes.title: Multiplicity additivity and associativity
nodes.statement: Fix D bounding the support dimensions of finite modules in 0→M′→M→M″→0. Then e_I^{[D]}(M)=e_I^{[D]}(M′)+e_I^{[D]}(M″). For nonzero M of intrinsic dimension d, e_I(M)=Σ_{p∈Supp M, dim A/p=d} length_{A_p}(M_p)·e_I(A/p); only the finitely many top-dimensional minimal support primes contribute. Intrinsic multiplicity is not additive when dimensions differ.
hypotheses: Fix D bounding the support dimensions of finite modules in 0→M′→M→M″→0.
proofSteps: Compare induced and intrinsic filtrations on M′ by Artin–Rees; the shift changes only lower polynomial coefficients.
Use a finite prime filtration. Fixed-D additivity kills lower-dimensional quotients, and localization counts occurrences of each top prime by module length.
acceptance: The cyclic quotient k of k[[t]] has intrinsic e=1 but contributes zero to the dimension-one associativity formula.

nodes.title: Completion and coefficient multiplicity comparisons
nodes.statement: Completion of finite local modules preserves Hilbert–Samuel functions and multiplicities. For flat local A→B with n_B=m_A B and residue extension a field, H_{m_B,M⊗B}=H_{m_A,M}; hence intrinsic and fixed-dimensional multiplicities agree. For a finite local map A→B and finite B-module N, length_A L=[k_B:k_A]length_B L for finite-length B-modules L; multiplicities for m_A and m_A B obey the same residue factor. Do not replace m_A B by m_B unless they are equal.
hypotheses: Completion of finite local modules preserves Hilbert–Samuel functions and multiplicities.
proofSteps: Identify every finite quotient after completion; flat scalar extension preserves the composition factors by extending the residue field.
For finite maps each residue B-factor has A-length [k_B:k_A], so sum composition lengths at each quotient precision and compare leading terms.
acceptance: For O⊂O′ ramified of index e, πO′=(π′)^e; e_{πO′}(O′)=e while e_{π′}(O′)=1.

nodes.title: Parameter length and Serre Euler characteristic
nodes.statement: For nonzero finite M of dimension d over Noetherian local A and a parameter list x of length d, all Koszul homologies H_i(x;M) have finite length and e_{(x)}(M)=Σ_i(−1)^i length H_i(x;M). Thus length(M/(x)M)≥e_{(x)}(M), with equality iff M is CM (equivalently x is M-regular). State this for the parameter ideal, not automatically for m.

The first partial Euler characteristic χ_1=length(M/(x)M)−e_{(x)}(M) is nonnegative and vanishes exactly when all positive Koszul homologies vanish. Use the supplier’s regular-sequence criterion.

nodes.title: Multiplicity one and regularity
nodes.statement: For a formally unmixed Noetherian local ring A, e_m(A)=1 iff A is regular. Formal unmixedness quantifies over every associated prime of Â and requires dim Â/p=dim A. For a regular local ring e_m(A)=1 without an extra unmixedness assumption. The converse in equal characteristic follows by completion, infinite residue extension and a minimal reduction; the general mixed-characteristic proof is a recorded source gap.
hypotheses: For a formally unmixed Noetherian local ring A, e_m(A)=1 iff A is regular.
proofSteps: Associativity and e=1 force one top associated prime with generic length one. Formal unmixedness removes all other associated primes and yields a domain.

In equal characteristic choose a minimal reduction, get a finite extension of a regular power-series ring of rank one, and use normality to identify the two rings. The general-characteristic extension is not supplied by the proof read.

nodes.title: Hilbert series and initial-form regularity
nodes.statement: For x∈m^r, r≥1, H_{A/(x)}(t)/(1−t)≥H_A(t)(1−t^r)/(1−t) coefficientwise. Equality in every degree implies x is A-regular; x being A-regular alone does not imply equality. Equality holds iff multiplication by x has the exact m-adic filtration condition; when x has order exactly r it is equivalent to its degree-r initial form being regular on gr_m A. For a genuinely graded ring and homogeneous x of degree r, equality is equivalent to x-regularity.
hypotheses: For x∈m^r, r≥1, H_{A/(x)}(t)/(1−t)≥H_A(t)(1−t^r)/(1−t) coefficientwise.
proofSteps: At each n compare the kernel of multiplication by x on A/m^{n+r}; it contains m^n/m^{n+r}.

Equality is the sharp kernel condition at every n. Krull intersection shows a nonzero annihilator of x makes some inequality strict. In the homogeneous case the grading makes the sharp condition equivalent to injectivity; in general compare with the associated graded initial form.
acceptance: In A=k[[t^6,t^7,t^15]], x=t^6 is regular, but t^15∈m∖m² and xt^15=t^21=(t^7)^3∈m³. Thus the initial class of x kills a nonzero degree-one class and the Hilbert inequality is strict.

nodes.title: Excellence and finite normalization
nodes.statement: Complete Noetherian local rings are excellent; localization and finite-type extension preserve excellence. An excellent reduced ring has finite normalization, and its local completion is reduced; normal excellent local rings have normal completions. Formal fibres of excellent rings are geometrically regular. Quasi-excellence is the G-ring plus J_2 condition, while excellence also includes universal catenarity. Ascent of formal-fibre S_n/CM conditions under finite type uses the corresponding quasi-excellence assumptions.
hypotheses: Complete Noetherian local rings are excellent; localization and finite-type extension preserve excellence.
proofSteps: Use the Cohen presentation and the excellence theorem for complete local rings, then stability under localization and finite type.

Apply the Nagata finiteness consequence to normalization. Use regular formal fibres for reduced/normal completion transfer; the finite-type formal-fibre statements factor through these fibre properties.
acceptance: Noetherianity alone does not imply finite normalization or reduced completion.

nodes.title: CM completion and catenary equidimensionality
nodes.statement: Finite M over Noetherian local A is CM iff its completion is CM; depth and support dimension are unchanged. A catenary S_2 Noetherian local ring is equidimensional. Excellence ensures universal catenarity and controls equidimensional completions. The finite normalization of a complete local reduced ring is a finite product of complete normal local domains.

proofSteps: Completion is faithfully flat with zero-dimensional field closed fibre; apply depth and dimension formulas.

Use the S_2 depth condition and catenary saturated chains to rule out different dimensions of local components. Finite algebras over a henselian complete ring split into their finitely many local factors.

nodes.title: CM and depth loci with dualizing complexes
nodes.statement: If a Noetherian ring A admits a dualizing complex, the set of primes p where a finite A-module M_p is Cohen–Macaulay is open in Supp M. More generally, depth conditions can be tested by the vanishing of the appropriate localized dual cohomology. For a flat map of Noetherian local rings, the S_n ascent target requires the base and every relevant fibre to satisfy S_n; descent holds for faithfully flat maps. Regular-locus openness over an excellent base is consumed from the existing ModularCurves target.
hypotheses: If a Noetherian ring A admits a dualizing complex, the set of primes p where a finite A-module M_p is Cohen–Macaulay is open in Supp M.
proofSteps: Use the bounded finite dual RHom_A(M,ω_A). Local duality identifies the CM condition with concentration in its local normalization degree.
Supports of finitely many unwanted dual cohomology modules are closed; stratify by the dimension/normalization degree and apply the dualizing dimension function to obtain openness on Supp M.
For S_n ascent and descent use the flat local depth and dimension formulas, checking all fibres at the primes in question.
acceptance: The theorem is not an unconditional CM-openness statement for every Noetherian ring without dualizing/formal-fibre input.

The characteristic-p hypothesis and module-finite meaning are part of the definition. For a field this is [k:k^p]<∞. Preserve F-finiteness under quotients, localization, finite-type extension and finite-variable formal power series over a Noetherian F-finite base.

nodes.title: Kunz criterion and henselian F-finiteness
nodes.statement: For a Noetherian ring A of characteristic p>0, A is regular iff Frobenius is flat. Under F-finiteness this is finite flatness, locally of rank p^{dim A} when the residue field is perfect. Henselization and strict henselization of an F-finite Noetherian ring remain F-finite; complete local rings with F-finite residue field are F-finite by a Cohen presentation.
hypotheses: For a Noetherian ring A of characteristic p>0, A is regular iff Frobenius is flat.
proofSteps: Work locally. Regular parameters and their pth powers give Frobenius flatness by the finite-module flatness criterion, with arbitrary residue-field Frobenius handled separately. Conversely Frobenius flatness makes a minimal generating set of m a regular sequence after Frobenius base change; the length comparison between F(m^n)A and m^{pn}, including the embedding-dimension shift, forces embedding dimension to equal dimension. Follow Stacks Local Cohomology 17.6.
For henselization use Frobenius base change along étale algebras and the filtered limit; a fixed Frobenius generating set survives. Complete rings reduce to finite-variable coefficient presentations.
acceptance: For imperfect residue k the rank includes [k:k^p]; it is not simply p^{dim A}.

A[1/π] is Jacobson; at each maximal ideal its residue is a finite extension of E and the associated map A→E′ lands in O_{E′}. nodes.title: Dimension over a punctured complete local spectrum
nodes.statement: For complete Noetherian local R and finite-type R-algebra S, the inverse image V of a nonempty open U⊂Spec R minus {m_R} is Jacobson. Its closed points map to coheight-one points of R with finite residue extensions. dim V≤dim U+max_{y closed in U}dim V_y. If every component of Spec S meets the closed fibre, its closure Z satisfies dim Z=dim V+1. Dominant finite-type maps of Noetherian Jacobson universally catenary schemes satisfy dim target≤dim source; over a complete local base the same conclusion holds when all source components meet the closed fibre.

nodes.title: Completed local rings after residue base change
nodes.statement: Let R be complete Noetherian local over O with residue k and A a finite-type R-algebra. For p∈Spec A put F=κ(p). Choose the coefficient ring Λ_F used at this point: Λ_F=F if F/E is finite, the unramified complete DVR with residue F if F/k is finite, and a Cohen DVR over O with residue F if F is a characteristic-p local field. Set B=Λ_F⊗_O A and q=ker(B→F), where λ⊗a maps to λ̄·(a mod p). If F is finite over E or k, B̂_q≅Â_p. If F is a characteristic-p local field, B̂_q≅Â_p[[T]]. In equal characteristic the latter is the diagonal completion of F⊗_k A. For the punctured-spectrum version explicitly require F finite over κ(p∩R); finite type alone does not imply this. The isomorphisms preserve regularity and CI, with the one-variable dimension increment retained.
hypotheses: Let R be complete Noetherian local over O with residue k and A a finite-type R-algebra.
proofSteps: The coefficient extension and local completion give a flat local Â_p-map. Compute the diagonal completed tensor of the coefficient ring with itself: it has one parameter for a characteristic-p local field, and none for a finite extension of k or E.
Lift that diagonal parameter T. The mod-π map is an isomorphism; flatness, separatedness and pseudocompact Nakayama make the completed map an isomorphism.
Use faithful flatness and formal-variable regularity/CI to compare the local properties. State the finite residue extension that the punctured proof needs.
acceptance: For A=R[x] and a nonclosed point above a coheight-one prime, κ(p)/κ(p∩R) can be transcendental; the finite-residue statement must not be used there.

nodes.title: Completed tensor domains and components
nodes.statement: Let A,B be complete Noetherian local O-flat domains with common residue k. Assume that both A[1/π] and B[1/π] are regular and that both A and B admit O-valued points. Then A⊗̂_O B is a domain and its generic fibre is regular. Separately, if A and B are reduced equidimensional O-flat complete local algebras, geometrically integral in the sense of Tho15 §1 (their scalar extensions to every finite coefficient extension remain domains), then their completed tensor product is geometrically integral of dimension dim A+dim B−1. For reduced equidimensional rings whose component quotients have this property, minimal primes of the completed tensor are indexed by pairs of minimal primes. Without that property, a component pair may split.
hypotheses: For the pointed KWII result, both domains are O-flat, both generic fibres are regular, and both rings admit O-valued points.
For the component-pair result, each component quotient is geometrically integral after every finite extension of the coefficient DVR, and the ambient rings are reduced, equidimensional and O-flat.
proofSteps: At both O-valued points, regularity embeds the domains into the completed local generic rings E[[x]] and E[[y]]. The coefficientwise tensor embedding and Chevalley topology comparison give a domain; the generic regularity comparison is KWII Proposition 2.2(ii).

For the geometric-integrality alternative and component pairs, use Tho15 Lemma 1.4(1),(2),(4): faithful flatness, the geometric integral-domain comparison, and contraction of minimal primes. The relative dimension is dim A+dim B−1.

Equivalently such an ideal is the intersection of kernels of its valued points. For a flat map of Noetherian schemes, the inverse image of a dense open is dense.

nodes.title: Torsion-free specialization at a coefficient point
nodes.statement: For a finite module M over complete local O-algebra A and a continuous point x:A→O′, define x^tf(M)=(M⊗_A O′)/(O′-torsion). This is finite free over O′. Maps induce functorial maps on these quotients; a torsion kernel before quotienting gives injection after quotienting. The projection of a finite O′-module to its torsion-free quotient splits noncanonically, so any additive functor preserves that split epimorphism.
hypotheses: For a finite module M over complete local O-algebra A and a continuous point x:A→O′, define x^tf(M)=(M⊗_A O′)/(O′-torsion).
proofSteps: The structure theorem over a DVR makes finite torsion-free modules free. Functoriality follows because a linear map takes torsion to torsion.

M is balanced if d_S(M)≥0. A minimal presentation S^b→S^a→M→0 has a=dim Tor_0 and b=dim Tor_1; balanced means b≤a. By adding zero relations it has a square presentation. This does not say that presentation is a resolution.

nodes.title: Balanced Taylor–Wiles module patching
nodes.statement: Let O have finite residue k, q≥1, S∞=O[[Z_p^q]], S_N=O[(Z/p^N)^q], and R∞=O[[x_1,…,x_{q−1}]]. Let R be CNL_O and H a finite R-module that is also finite over O. For each N there are φ_N:R∞↠R and a finite S_N-module H_N, balanced over the local ring S_N, with a compatible R∞-action. Require that the S_N-action lies in the image of R∞, that its augmentation ideal acts through the image of ker φ_N, and that H_N/(augmentation)H_N≅H as R∞-modules via φ_N. Then H is finite free over R. Patch finite open quotients, uniformly bounded square presentations and all these maps. H=0 is allowed; the nonzero proof uses dim R∞=dim S∞−1.

Its support has codimension at least one. The determinant of the square matrix is nonzero; injectivity gives pd≤1. AB and the finite action image force depth_R∞=dim R∞, hence R∞-freeness.
Augment S∞ and identify H as a free module over the quotient R supplied by the surjection and annihilator comparison.

nodes.title: Regular-base patching and full support
nodes.statement: Let S→R be a local homomorphism of Noetherian local rings, with S regular of finite dimension d. Let 0≤l≤d and let M≠0 be an R-module finite over both S and R, with the S-action induced by S→R. If dim R≤d−l and M admits an S-free resolution of length≤l, then depth_S M=depth_R M=dim Supp_R M=dim R=d−l; in particular M is MCM over R. If R is a domain, M is nearly faithful; if R is regular, M is finite free. No full-support conclusion follows for a reducible R from these dimension equalities alone.
hypotheses: S→R is local Noetherian, S is regular of dimension d, 0≤l≤d, M≠0 is finite over S and R with compatible actions, dim R≤d−l, and pd_S M≤l.
proofSteps: AB gives depth_S M≥d−l, while finite-image dimension comparison bounds dim Supp M by dim R. All inequalities become equalities.
For a domain a closed support of full dimension contains its generic point and hence every point. Over regular R AB gives pd=0. Reducible cases require the component-support input from R03.6.
acceptance: A/(x) over A=k[[x,y]]/(xy) is full-dimensional MCM but misses the component (y); domain/full-support qualifications matter.

nodes.title: Characteristic-zero module patching over open quotients
nodes.statement: Let O have finite residue k, Λ=O[[w_1,…,w_s]], T=Λ[[z_1,…,z_t]], Δ_N=(Z/p^N)^q, S_N=T[Δ_N] and S∞=T[[Z_p^q]]. Let R_N be complete Noetherian local S_N-algebras with continuous Λ-algebra surjections R∞↠R_N from one complete Noetherian local Λ-algebra R∞. Let F_N be finite free S_N-modules of one rank r, with R_N-actions whose restriction along S_N→R_N is the scalar S_N-action. Require compatible Λ-linear identifications F_N/(z,augmentation)F_N≅M, with M Λ-free of rank r, and compatible quotient maps R_N/(z,augmentation)↠R acting on M. Stabilize the modules, ring truncations, coefficient maps, action maps and augmentation maps over a countable cofinal family of open S∞-ideals containing powers of its entire maximal ideal. Then obtain M∞ finite free of rank r over S∞, a quotient Rpatch of R∞ acting on it, a coefficient map S∞→Rpatch, M∞/(z,augmentation)M∞≅M, and Rpatch/(z,augmentation)↠R. One can take F_N=T⊗̂_Λ M_N from free Λ[Δ_N]-modules when compatible framed R_N-actions are supplied. Generic freeness over R∞ additionally requires pointwise regularity and the dimension equality in the regular-base criterion; these conditions are not supplied by finite-quotient stabilization.
hypotheses: Let O have finite residue k, Λ=O[[w_1,…,w_s]], T=Λ[[z_1,…,z_t]], Δ_N=(Z/p^N)^q, S_N=T[Δ_N] and S∞=T[[Z_p^q]].

The resulting coefficient module is free of rank r since its compatible finite quotients are free of that rank; completeness gives M∞.
Take the limit of the finite quotient images of R∞, retaining the S∞-map and augmentation. Finite inverse-limit exactness preserves the surjections.
acceptance: For positive-dimensional T, S_N is finite over T but has infinitely many elements; an open ideal containing a power of the entire maximal ideal is needed for finite pigeonhole arguments.
An R_N-action commuting with coefficients must also restrict to the scalar S_N-action; commutation alone does not establish that compatibility.

nodes.statement: In the preceding characteristic-zero patching data, let compatible Λ-points R_N→O, R∞→O and Rpatch→O have kernels q_N,q∞,qpatch. Assume π^d annihilates q_N/(q_N²+q∞R_N) for one fixed d at every finite level. Retain these point maps in the finite truncations and use one uniform finite set of generators for the relative cotangent images, so that the inverse limit computes qpatch/(qpatch²+q∞Rpatch). Then π^d annihilates that patched cotangent module. After inverting π its localization at the point is zero. If the completed local map from R∞ to Rpatch at this point has the same residue field, the zero relative cotangent and completeness make that completed map surjective. If the source completion is regular of dimension dim(S∞[1/π] at its contracted point), and M∞ has that depth, Auslander–Buchsbaum makes its corresponding finite module free over the source completion; augmentation yields the claimed characteristic-zero freeness for M. nodes.title: Projectivity tested by derived coinvariants
nodes.statement: Let A be Noetherian local with residue characteristic p, G a finite group, H a Sylow p-subgroup and M a finite A[G]-module. nodes.title: Component support and augmentation
nodes.statement: A nonzero finite MCM module over Noetherian local A has support a union of top-dimensional components. If A is a domain it is nearly faithful. A finite nearly faithful module remains so after a proper quotient; completion preserves this. If M is O-flat and p is minimal in Supp(M/πM), p is not minimal in Supp M. nodes.title: Connectedness dimension
nodes.statement: For a nonzero Noetherian local ring A of dimension d, define c(A) as the minimum of d and the dimensions of intersections of the two closed unions from all nonempty partitions of its irreducible components. Thus an irreducible spectrum has c(A)=d; dim empty=−1. Equivalently c(A) is the least dimension of a closed subset whose complement is disconnected, with the whole-space convention d. Define arithmetic rank ara(I) as the least number of elements generating an ideal with radical √I.

proofSteps: Use the finite component set; include d in the minimum so empty partition sets have a finite value.
Match the partition intersections with complements of separating closed subsets. Define arithmetic rank through radical equality, using the pinned finite ideal generation.

nodes.title: Specialization cycles and Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity
nodes.statement: Use SF.5’s fixed-dimensional cycle Z_D(M)=Σ_{dim A/p=D}length_{A_p}(M_p)[p]. Let A be equidimensional, complete and O-flat of dimension d+1, and M finite and O-flat. Cartier specialization gives Z_d(M/πM)=Σ_{p∈Min A}length_{A_p}(M_p) Z_d((A/p)/π), with zero coefficients allowed. These coefficients are generic lengths; they are generic ranks when A is generically reduced. Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity in a fixed dimension is the cycle-weighted sum of e_m(A/p), with smaller-dimensional terms contributing zero. Distinct generic components with disjoint special-cycle support and coefficient-one specializations allow equality with a full-support special module to determine positive integral generic lengths. Calling those integers ranks additionally requires generically reduced A.

proofSteps: Apply the Cartier specialization map to the generic-length cycle of M. Additivity and π-regularity express the special cycle as the stated sum of reduced component specialization cycles.
Apply multiplicity associativity in a fixed ambient dimension. With coefficient-one specializations and disjoint cycle support, each generic length is read separately as a positive integer.

nodes.title: Square-free monomial components and cycles
nodes.statement: In k[[u_1,…,u_n]], a square-free monomial ideal is radical; its minimal primes are the coordinate ideals from the minimal vertex covers of its support hypergraph. If all covers have size c, the quotient is equidimensional of dimension n−c and each component has generic length one. Multiplicity equals the number of these coordinate components. In the LLHLM20 Lemma 3.6.13 example rename the six coordinates a,b,c,d,e,f; its ideal is (ab,ac,ae,bc,bd,cf), whose minimal primes are (a,b,c), (a,b,f), (a,c,d), (b,c,e). Thus the ring is reduced of dimension three and has multiplicity four. The coordinate change is a=c12−c13c32, b=κc31−c21c32, c=c23, d=c13, e=c21, f=c32, with κ≠0. This component computation does not assert CM for every square-free monomial quotient.
hypotheses: In k[[u_1,…,u_n]], a square-free monomial ideal is radical; its minimal primes are the coordinate ideals from the minimal vertex covers of its support hypergraph.
proofSteps: Membership of a monomial in a coordinate prime is combinatorial; intersect minimal cover ideals to recover exactly the square-free monomial ideal.
Each localized coordinate component is a field, giving coefficient one. The multiplicity associativity formula counts components.
acceptance: k[[x,y]]/(x²y) is monomial but not square-free and is not reduced; it is excluded.

A point A→O′ sends an actual global ideal J_A to the generated ideal x(J_A) on the torsion-free rank-one specialization; for a nonzero image this is π′^v O′. nodes.title: CM Hilbert-series surjection criterion
nodes.statement: Let M↠N be a surjection of finite graded modules over a standard graded k-algebra, or finite filtered modules with good separated filtrations for which the surjection is strict. Equality of Hilbert series implies the map is an isomorphism: its graded kernel has every piece zero. Separately, for a surjection of nonzero finite modules over a Noetherian local ring, if M is CM, dim Supp N=dim Supp M=d and their intrinsic m-multiplicities agree, the map is an isomorphism. Indeed every nonzero submodule of CM M has dimension d, and fixed-dimensional multiplicity additivity would give a positive kernel contribution. Without CM or a same-dimensional associated-prime condition, equal multiplicities can miss an embedded lower-dimensional kernel.

proofSteps: Exact graded pieces make the kernel series zero. For strict filtered maps compare associated graded and use separatedness.
For the multiplicity variant, a nonzero submodule of an unmixed CM module has full dimension and positive multiplicity, contradicting equal leading coefficients.

nodes.statement: For an O-module P with no π-torsion, P/π^nP is free over O/π^n, allowing infinite rank. A completed infinite free module is the completion of a direct sum supplied by PadicMeasures L0, not an unrestricted algebraic product.

For arbitrary projectives, decompose a projective module into a transfinite direct sum of countably generated projectives using the split free presentation. Over a local ring a countably generated projective is free by successive basis extraction. This is Stacks Algebra 84.5 and 85.1–85.4; finite Nakayama alone does not prove it.

nodes.title: Exactness of cofiltered finite limits
nodes.statement: For a complete Noetherian local A, inverse limits over any cofiltered diagram of finite A-modules are exact. With enhanced derived/homotopy limits, uniformly bounded diagrams of complexes having finite cohomology satisfy H^i(holim C_j)≅lim H^i(C_j). proofSteps: Matlis duality turns finite modules into Artinian modules and exchanges cofiltered limits with filtered colimits. Exact filtered colimits and faithful biduality give exactness.
Use enhanced limit resolutions and exactness to collapse the associated derived-limit spectral sequence for bounded finite cohomology.

nodes.title: Nilpotence of the ghost ideal
nodes.statement: For C∈D(A) with cohomology only in [a,b], let J⊂End_D(C) be endomorphisms acting as zero on all H^i(C). Then J^{b−a+1}=0. Hence a finite derived action with cohomologically trivial kernel has a uniformly nilpotent kernel bounded by cohomological range.
hypotheses: For C∈D(A) with cohomology only in [a,b], let J⊂End_D(C) be endomorphisms acting as zero on all H^i(C).
proofSteps: Filter C by its cohomological truncations. A ghost lowers the filtration one step; a product of b−a+1 ghosts factors through zero.
Use the kernel of the product cohomology-action map as the ideal and carry the exponent into each finite quotient.
acceptance: For C concentrated in one cohomology degree the ghost ideal is zero; the exponent becomes one.

nodes.title: Localization of finite derived actions
nodes.statement: For perfect C over Noetherian A, any A-subalgebra T of End_D(A)(C) is finite as an A-module. If p is a minimal prime of T and q=p∩A, pT_q is both minimal and maximal. Hence T_q≅T_p×B, with T_p an isolated Artinian block. Its idempotent splits C⊗_A A_q in the derived category, giving C_p with H^i(C_p)=H^i(C)_p. For the special fibre modulo f, a maximal prime m of T/f whose localization has dimension zero is likewise minimal and gives an isolated block in the finite A/f-algebra. An arbitrary prime of T need not define such a splitting.
hypotheses: For perfect C over Noetherian A, any A-subalgebra T of End_D(A)(C) is finite as an A-module.
proofSteps: The finite Hom complex for C makes End_D(C) finite over A, and Noetherianity makes T finite. Integral incomparability makes a minimal p maximal after localizing A at q.
A prime that is both maximal and minimal in a Noetherian spectrum is an isolated component: split the reduced ring along that component, then lift its idempotent through the nilradical.
Split the induced derived idempotent through the enhanced supplier. Exact cohomology identifies its image with localization at p; repeat for the zero-dimensional maximal block of T/f.
acceptance: Localization at p is performed on the action and its idempotent block; writing a strict C⊗_T T_p would assume missing strict T-linearity.

nodes.title: Finite ultraproduct localization
nodes.statement: Let A be a finite commutative local ring with maximal ideal m_A and fix one nonprincipal ultrafilter F on N. Evaluation ev_F:∏_N A→A assigns the unique F-large constant value. Put x_F=ev_F^{-1}(m_A); this is a maximal ideal, and (∏ A)_{x_F}≅A. Localization of product modules there is exact. Products of finite free A-modules whose ranks are uniformly bounded are finite projective over ∏ A, using the finitely many rank idempotents; localization selects one rank. This functor commutes with finitely presented coefficient quotients, finite-projective duals and bounded-complex cohomology. If A is a field, x_F is the kernel of ev_F; this kernel description is not used for a general local ring.

proofSteps: A finite partition has exactly one F-large cell, defining the coefficient specialization. Invert sequences which are units on that cell.
Partition indices by rank and choose bases on each part, making the product a finite projective module. Exact products followed by exact localization preserve complexes and their cohomology.

nodes.statement: Let S be a power-series ring over a complete DVR, C,C′ perfect over S of Tor amplitude [a,a+l], with identified mod-π reductions and equal finite Hecke image there. Let R,R′ be complete Noetherian local S-algebras with surjections onto their finite action images modulo uniformly nilpotent ideals, and identify R/π≅R′/π compatibly on special cohomology modulo the sum of those ideals. Put D=dim S−l. Assume dim R=dim R′=D, dim(R/π)=dim(R′/π)=D−1; each top-dimensional special generic point of R/π lies on exactly one D-dimensional R-component; R′ has exactly one D-dimensional component; every other generic component of R,R′,R/π has dimension<D−1. Finally at some characteristic-zero coheight-one p⊃a∞ in S, C⊗^L κ(p)≠0 has cohomology only in [a,a+l]. Then the R-spectrum support of H^*(C) contains every D-dimensional component. Support is transported through Spec T≅Spec(T/I)→Spec R, not a fictitious R-module structure.

existingContracts.title: Hilbert–Samuel multiplicity
existingContracts.statement: For Noetherian local (A,m), finite M and an m-primary ideal I, define H_{I,M}(n)=length_A(M/I^{n+1}M), n≥0. There is a unique eventual polynomial P_{I,M}∈Q[T]; for M≠0 it has degree d=dim Supp M and positive leading coefficient. Define intrinsic e_I(M)=d!·coeff_d(P), an integer >0 for M≠0, and e_I(0)=0. Separately, for D≥dim Supp M, define e_I^{[D]}(M)=D!·coeff_D(P), including the zero polynomial; it is zero when dim Supp M<D and agrees with intrinsic e when equality holds. Write e(M)=e_m(M) only when the intrinsic convention is intended. Define the associated-graded Hilbert function h(n)=length(I^nM/I^{n+1}M), so H(n)=Σ_{j=0}^n h(j); h has degree d−1 for d>0. The factorial attached to h is (d−1)!, not d!.
hypotheses: A is Noetherian local; M is finite; radical I=m. Thus I is proper and M/IM has finite length.
Intrinsic degree is dim Supp M; the ambient-dimension variant uses a separately chosen D≥dim Supp M. The zero module has multiplicity zero.
proofSteps: Use the finite associated graded module over gr_I A and a finite degree-one polynomial presentation to obtain eventual polynomiality; successive differences convert graded lengths to the cumulative function.

Use prime filtrations, Artin–Rees and parameter dimension bounds to identify the degree with support dimension. The integer-valued polynomial/binomial basis gives positivity and integrality of the factorial-scaled leading coefficient.
Define a separate coefficient-at-D operation before stating additive or cycle identities, so modules of smaller dimension contribute zero rather than their intrinsic multiplicity.
acceptance: For A=k[[x,y]], H(n)=binom(n+2,2), d=2, e(A)=1; h(n)=n+1.
For A=k[t]/t^r, H(n)=min(n+1,r), d=0, e(A)=r.
For A=k[[x,y]], M=A/(x): intrinsic e(M)=1, while e_m^{[2]}(M)=0.
H_{I,0}=0 and both intrinsic and ambient multiplicities are zero.
For k of characteristic zero and A=k[[x,y]]/(y²−x³), H(n)=2n+1 for n≥0 and e=2.
For A=k[[x,y]]/(xy), H(n)=2n+1 and e=2; its two components each have e=1.
For A=k[[x,y]]/(y³−x⁴) over characteristic zero, H(n)=3n for n≥1 and e=3.
In 0→(x)→k[[x]]→k→0, intrinsic multiplicities are 1,1,1 and do not add; at D=1 the k term has multiplicity zero.
For A=k[[x,y]]/(xy,y²), H(n)=n+2 for n≥1 and e=1, but embedding dimension is two and A is not regular. Its embedded associated prime violates formal unmixedness.
For A=k[[x,y]], e_{m²}(A)=4, so the defining ideal cannot be ignored.
For A=k[[x,y]]/(y), H(n)=n+1 and e(A)=1.
In characteristic zero, A=k[[x,y]]/(y²−x²(x+1)) has initial equation y²−x², H(n)=2n+1 and e(A)=2.
In characteristic zero, A=k[[x,y]]/(x³−y³) has H(n)=3n for n≥1 and e(A)=3. Over an algebraically closed field its three distinct linear branches each contribute one.

Cohen coefficients and compatible coefficient embeddings are distinguished from arbitrary functorial choices of coefficient fields. Source: Andre18, §4.2 and §4.4(1), printed pp. 86–88.
Finite parameter subrings use a system of parameters in the complete local setting; the dimension and topology conditions are essential. Source: Andre18, §4.2, printed p. 86.
Perfect residue extensions require the stated coefficient compatibility; coefficient change is not automatic for an arbitrary residue field. Source: Andre18, §4.2 and §4.4(1), printed pp. 86–88.

The completed tensor carrier retains its coefficient ring and maximal topology; ordinary tensor and generic localization are separate comparisons. Source: KWII, §2.1–2.3, pp. 6–10; CG18 Lemma 4.2, p. 355.
Completion of arbitrary flat algebras imports the accepted owner and retains Noetherian base and finite-generator topology hypotheses. Source: Andre18, Lemma 1.1.1 and proof, printed pp. 75–76.
PQ26 Lemma 5.15 gives maximal-adic quotient completion for finitely generated J when the completion is Noetherian; arbitrary adic exactness was removed. Source: PQ26, Lemma 5.15, p. 34.
The pro-zero kernel/cokernel condition is an eventual condition at every precision, not a levelwise isomorphism. Source: Bhatt18, Lemma 5.3, PDF pp. 9–10.
The accepted adic-Hom owner is reused; finite modules and Mittag–Leffler comparisons control the stated lim¹ rather than a general vanishing claim. Source: Bhatt18, Lemma 5.3, PDF pp. 9–10.

Chevalley comparison uses complete Noetherian local modules and a separated descending filtration; the comparison need not have a linear rate. Source: KWII, Proof of Proposition 2.2(ii), p. 9; Hochster11 Matlis duality §5.

Schlessinger conditions specify which fibre squares require surjectivity or bijectivity, with tangent finiteness separate. Source: StacksFormalDefos, §10, pp. 26–28; §12, pp. 32–35; Remark 13.5, p. 41; Remark 15.6, p. 47.

A hull is versal and tangent-minimal; its smooth natural transformation is distinguished from a representing isomorphism. Source: StacksFormalDefos, Definitions 8.9 and 14.4, pp. 23 and 44; Lemma 14.5, p. 44; Remark 15.6, p. 47.
The finite tangent hypothesis and small-extension lifting conditions are retained in the hull theorem. Source: StacksFormalDefos, Lemma 13.4 and Remark 13.5, pp. 39–41; Theorem 15.5, pp. 46–47.

The automorphism/Rim–Schlessinger obstruction is explicitly stronger than existence of a hull; it supplies the prorepresentability comparison. Source: StacksFormalDefos, Lemmas 16.3 and 16.7, pp. 48–51; Lemma 18.1 and Theorem 18.2, pp. 54–55.

The obstruction space is complete and functorial for the stated extensions; full cotangent complexes are requested from their owner. Source: StacksFormalDefos, Lemma 17.5 and Remark 17.6, pp. 53–54; Definition 9.1 and warning, p. 24.

The relation bound remains conditional on the complete obstruction setup and has an explicit unread primary-proof refinement; no arithmetic dual-Selmer identity is supplied here. Source: StacksFormalDefos, §§13 and 17, pp. 39–41 and 53–54; KWII §2.2, pp. 7–8.

Framing is formally smooth with a specified relative dimension and chosen coordinates; it is not a canonical presentation of every hull. Source: KWII, Proposition 2.1 and following discussion, pp. 7–8; Stacks Lemma 14.5, p. 44.

Depth of zero is extended infinite and grade uses the stated ideal; the regular-sequence and Ext characterizations retain finite-module assumptions. Source: StacksDualizing, Lemma 11.1, pp. 18–19, tag 0AVZ; Stacks Algebra §72.

Secant sequences, systems of parameters and CM-secant sequences are distinguished; the definition does not assert every parameter sequence is regular. Source: Ces21, Definition 3.1 and Remark 3.2, PDF pp. 9–10; André §0.1, printed p. 72.

Height and quotient dimension inequalities retain Noetherian and finite-module conditions; equality is a separate parameter/CM statement. Source: StacksAlgebra, §60 (dimension), §103 (CM), pp. 140–145 and 246–251; IKM24 Lemma 3.1, p. 17.

CM uses support dimension, while MCM and full support are distinct; a component module tests the difference. Source: StacksAlgebra, Definitions 103.1 and 103.8, pp. 246 and 248, tags 00N3 and 00NF; LLHLM20 Definition 3.5.1, p. 37.

The depth lemma uses finite modules and exact sequences; CM associated primes are minimal in support, not automatically all ambient minimal primes. Source: StacksDualizing, Lemma 11.2, p. 19, tag 0BUV; Stacks Algebra Lemma 103.7, pp. 247–248, tag 0BUS.

Rank for finite-projective-dimension modules comes from finite resolutions at the specified generic points; finite-support Euler theory is imported. Source: Andre18, §0.1, footnote 1, printed p. 72.
Serre depth conditions are local support conditions; formal unmixedness is imposed on completion and is not equated with reducedness. Source: EGA2, §6.4, printed pp. 141–142; Stone Theorem 16, p. 20.
Local and relative complete intersections retain regular-presentation hypotheses and reuse the imported Koszul carrier. Source: IKM24, §9, p. 40; PQ26 Lemma 3.9, p. 22; Ces19 Corollary 2.5, p. 5.
The dimension-count complete-intersection criterion includes coefficient flatness/regularity needed to turn the chosen equations into a regular sequence. Source: PQ26, Lemma 3.9, p. 22.

CM completion and catenary equidimensionality retain the full-support/equidimensional hypotheses; they are not assertions about every Noetherian local ring. Source: Ces21, Lemma 2.5 proof, PDF p. 6; André §4.3–4.4, printed pp. 87–88; Stacks tags 07NX and 07NZ.

CM and depth locus openness uses the existence of a dualizing complex and the specified finite modules; the existing regular-locus comparison is imported. Source: StacksDualizing, Lemma 20.4, p. 37, tag 0EHS; Ces21 §3.5, PDF p. 10.

F-finiteness is finiteness of Frobenius with its twisted scalar action; the examples distinguish finite coefficients from unrestricted perfect extensions. Source: CMM21, Definition 5.1, p. 38; Example 6.7, p. 53; BM23 §4.4, Corollary 4.20 and proof, PDF pp. 20–21.

Kunz is stated in characteristic p, and the henselian F-finite comparison retains the coefficient hypotheses; BM23’s locator was corrected to §4.4. Source: CMM21, Example 6.7, p. 53 and Lemma 5.29 proof, p. 46; BM23 §4.4 before Corollary 4.20, PDF pp. 20–21.

Ring lci/syntomic criteria retain their local-presentation and flat-fibre hypotheses; generic geometric definitions are an additional SF.4 request, not claimed present. Source: Ces19, Corollary 2.5, pp. 5–6; Stacks tags 0E9K, 069I, 07D3 and 09Q7.

Topological Nakayama lifts a finite parameter quotient to module finiteness; finite action images alone do not satisfy that whole-ring hypothesis. Source: Kisin09, §3.3, pp. 1157–1159; IKM24 proof of Theorem 10.6, pp. 46–47.

Generic Jacobson and valued-point conclusions use complete Noetherian O-algebras and finite coefficient extensions; points are not restricted to O itself. Source: BIP23, Lemma 3.17, PDF p. 18; KWII Proposition 2.2(i) and Corollary 2.3, pp. 9–10.

Punctured-base dimension retains the residue/transcendence terms; BIP’s finite-type versus finite-algebraic field issue is not silently used. Source: BIP23, Lemmas 3.14 and 3.18–3.20, PDF pp. 16–19; PQ26 Lemma 14.2 and Remark 14.3, pp. 72–73.

Completed local residue change uses the actual field extension and completed tensor, with generic dimensions separated from ordinary finite-type base change. Source: BIP23, Lemmas 3.35–3.37, PDF pp. 27–28 (published pp. 24–25).

The KWII domain theorem now requires both regular generic fibres and both O-valued points; Thorne’s geometric-integrality alternative supplies component pairs and dimension separately. Source: KWII, Proposition 2.2(ii) and proof, pp. 9–10.

Reduced flat quotient identification uses valued points over all specified finite coefficient extensions; a single rational point does not determine the quotient. Source: KWII, Corollary 2.3, pp. 9–10; BIP23 Lemma 3.54, PDF p. 34.

Torsion-free specialization is quotienting by coefficient torsion before rank/length calculations, with no unjustified preservation of injections. Source: IKM24, §2.1, p. 13; LLHLM20 before (5.9), published p. 126.

Regular parameters compute the residue Ext exterior algebra through the imported Koszul complex; regularity is essential. Source: IKM24, Lemma 2.6 proof, pp. 15–16; §§3 and 6.6, pp. 18–19 and 29; Stacks Algebra §110.

Coset prime avoidance is for finitely many primes with the stated ideal exclusions; it lifts parameters without imposing CM where only avoidance is used. Source: IKM24, Proofs of Theorem 5.6, Lemma 9.4 and Theorem 9.6, pp. 25 and 39–41; §2.2, p. 13.

Balanced modules use generator-minus-relation defect and finite residue Tor groups; the tests distinguish a balanced module from a free one. Source: CG18, Definitions 2.1–2.2 and Proposition 2.3 proof, pp. 307–310.

The defect/coinvariant formula uses the exact Tor/coinvariant sequence and the finite group algebra coefficient structure. Source: CG18, Proposition 3.8 proof, p. 323; Proposition 5.10 proof, p. 378; CG20 Theorem 7.11 proof, p. 853.
Balanced Taylor–Wiles patching retains finite separated H, bounded level precision, a common ring map and compatible augmentations. Source: CG18, Proposition 2.3 and proof, pp. 308–310.

The regular-base criterion now states nonzero compatible finite modules, 0≤l≤d and all depth/support-dimension equalities; nearly faithful is only concluded in the domain case. Source: Kisin09, §3.3.1–3.3.4, published pp. 1157–1159; BCGP25 Proposition 7.2.3 and proof, pp. 162–163.

Open-quotient patching now specifies S_N-algebras and actions extending scalar coefficients, fixed free rank and whole-maximal-ideal cofinal finite truncations. Source: BCGP25, §7.2.1 and the patching construction, pp. 161–163.

Uniform cotangent annihilation retains finite generation, pointed coefficient maps and the explicit inverse-limit comparison as hypotheses and a recorded refinement. Source: BCGP25, Lemma 7.2.2 and proof, p. 162.

Projectivity is tested by derived coinvariants under the finite group-algebra hypotheses; ordinary coinvariants alone would miss higher Tor. Source: BCGP25, Lemma 7.3.2, p. 165; Lemma 7.4.11 proof, p. 172.

Nearly faithful is annihilator nilpotence/full support for finite Noetherian modules; its completion API now specifies faithfully flat maximal-adic completion. Source: Tho15, Lemma 1.10(2), p. 8; Kisin09 §3.3.4, p. 1159.

The maximal O-flat quotient kills all π-power torsion, rather than just elements killed by π; the torsion ideal and universal map are tested. Source: BCGP21, §7.11 before (7.11.1), published pp. 425–426.

Full-support and augmentation conclusions preserve component and nonzero support hypotheses; MCM does not imply nearly faithful on a reducible ring. Source: Tho15, Lemma 1.10, p. 8; Kisin09 §3.3.4, p. 1159.
Connectedness uses the capped convention in irreducible cases and records the mismatch with Thorne’s literal infimum convention. Source: Tho15, Definition 1.7 and Proposition 1.8, p. 8.

The relation connectedness bound retains the capped-convention comparison and explicitly records the unread Brodmann–Rung proof. Source: Tho15, Proposition 1.8, p. 8, citing Brodmann–Rung Theorem 2.4.

Generic/special component comparisons retain O-flatness, equidimensionality and the specified completed base changes; no bijection is claimed for arbitrary reduction. Source: Tho15, Proposition 1.6 and proof, p. 7; ACC23 Proposition 6.3.8 and Corollary 6.3.9, published pp. 1052–1053.

Cartier specialization coefficients are now generic lengths; rank language is restricted to generically reduced rings, and O[ε]/ε² tests the distinction. Source: BCGP21, §7.12, (7.12.1), Lemmas 7.12.2–7.12.3 and Remarks 7.12.6–7.12.7, published pp. 427–430; EG14 Proposition 2.2.10 and Lemma 2.2.13, pp. 8–9.

Completed-tensor multiplicity uses common residue fields and the geometrically integral/reduced component assumptions; split component products are not replaced by a single prime. Source: EG14, Lemma 2.2.14, arXiv v3 p. 9; LLHLM20 Corollary 3.5.5 proof, p. 39; BCGP21 (7.12.1), p. 427.

Square-free monomial ideals are reduced intersections of coordinate primes; the six-variable example checks the four components without asserting arbitrary such quotients are CM. Source: LLHLM20, Proof of Lemma 3.6.13, published pp. 70–71.

Depth-two extension controls the global image only when that image also has the extension property; specialization of an injection requires separate Tor/saturation input. Source: LLHLM20, Lemmas 5.2.1–5.2.2, Theorem 5.2.3, Remark 5.2.4, pp. 119–120; proof of Theorem 5.3.5, p. 126.

Formal-variable extension of crossing loci and ideals keeps finite depth-two extension and geometric reducedness hypotheses; imperfect-field tensor counterexamples are excluded. Source: LLHLM20, Before Lemma 5.2.1 and Remark 5.2.4, pp. 119–120; proof of Proposition 5.1.8, p. 118.
The CM Hilbert-series criterion uses a standard graded CM source, equal graded dimensions and the correct initial-form regularity condition. Source: LLHLM20, Lemma 3.6.11 and proof, published p. 69.

Perfectness means bounded finite-projective models, not merely bounded cohomology; Tor-amplitude tests and the explicit More on Algebra source support the adapter. Source: BP26, Lemma 2.6.6, pp. 21–22; KT17 §2.1, pp. 5–6; Stacks More on Algebra §perfect complexes.

Minimal models use local cancellation and existing K-projective comparison APIs; quasi-isomorphisms between minimal finite models become degreewise isomorphisms. Source: KT17, §2.1–§2.3, Lemmas 2.3 and 2.5, pp. 5–7; IKM24 proof of Theorem 10.6, pp. 44–45.
Residue exactness yields exactness at the middle of three finite free terms, with no false endpoint injectivity conclusion. Source: BP26, Lemma 2.6.6, pp. 21–22.

Uniformly bounded-below targets make the pseudo-coherent filtered-Hom adapter valid; the BP26 application satisfies that bound and its purported source error is rejected. Source: BP26, Proposition 2.3.13 proof, p. 17.

Coefficient reductions use completed direct sums/topological bases; arbitrary infinite products are excluded and the required L0 interface is explicitly requested. Source: CG18, Lemmas 7.5–7.7 and proof, pp. 396–398; Pilloni20 §2.3, pp. 9–11.

Bounded flat complete complexes require finite residue cohomology and topological freeness comparisons; bounded cohomology alone is not a perfectness theorem. Source: Pilloni20, Proposition 2.2.1, author p. 9; Lemma 2.3.1 and the splitting argument in Proposition 2.3.1, author p. 10.

Fixed finite ranks and strict cocycle comparisons yield finite perfect inverse limits; uniqueness is in the derived category and uses the pinned K-projective Hom comparison. Source: KT17, Lemmas 2.13–2.14, pp. 11–12; ACC23 §6.4, published pp. 1058–1060.
Cofiltered exactness uses finite coefficient sets and Mittag–Leffler, with the lim¹ obstruction visible outside those conditions. Source: BMP23, Lemma 4.10 and Remarks 4.11–4.12, pp. 39–40.

A derived ring action is a map into a derived endomorphism ring, not a strict chain-module structure; the restriction and morphism compatibility tests enforce this. Source: IKM24, 10.2, p. 42; ACC23 §6.3.1, published p. 1047.

Ghost nilpotence has a uniform exponent controlled by the bounded cohomological range; it is not an injectivity assertion on endomorphisms. Source: KT17, Lemmas 2.3 and 2.5, pp. 6–7; ACC23 Lemma 6.3.2, published p. 1047.
Two-term detection uses both ordinary and dual endpoints; one endpoint alone loses nonzero ghost maps. Source: IKM24, Lemma 10.8 and proof, pp. 48–49.

Finite derived-action localization uses idempotent splitting from the enhanced presentability request and bounded summands; formal Karoubi completion does not prove splitting in the original category. Source: ACC23, §6.3.1–§6.3.3, published pp. 1047–1049.

The elementary DVR coefficient dual is Hom_O(−,E/O), with the two-term O–E comparison and degree conventions, not ordinary Hom into O. Source: BCGP21, Lemmas 7.8.5–7.8.6 and Remark 7.8.7, published pp. 411–412.

Finite patching coefficients are now explicitly module-finite over Λ; finite cardinality is achieved only after whole-maximal-ideal truncation. Source: ACC23, §6.4.1–§6.4.6, published pp. 1053–1055; IKM24 10.1–10.4, pp. 42–43.

Finite ultraproduct localization requires uniformly bounded cardinality over a fixed finite ring and a single nonprincipal ultrafilter; merely finitely generated modules are insufficient. Source: GN, §2.2, Lemmas 2.2.2–2.2.6 and Corollary 2.2.7, pp. 12–13; IKM24 proof of Theorem 10.6, p. 44.

Ultrapatching uses fixed term ranks, finite matrices, one ultrafilter and compatible transition data; homotopy classes, not strict unique lifts, carry the morphisms. Source: ACC23, Propositions 6.4.10, 6.4.12 and 6.4.16; Remark 6.4.13, published pp. 1056–1060; IKM24 Theorem 10.6 proof, pp. 44–46.

The patched coefficient map is lifted once through Q and used for every object; no unproved whole-ring finiteness is used by the action construction. Source: ACC23, Remark 6.4.8, Proposition 6.4.12(3), Remark 6.4.14 and Lemma 6.4.15, published pp. 1056–1059; IKM24 Theorem 10.6 proof, pp. 44 and 46–47.

Paired systems share ultrafilter, residue identifications and mod-π action maps; arbitrary independently chosen limits do not provide paired actions. Source: ACC23, Remark 6.4.14 and Proposition 6.4.17, published pp. 1059–1061.

The genuine-action patching functor uses codimension/amplitude equality and a nonzero input for MCM conclusions; top augmentation is separated from derived augmentation. Source: IKM24, Theorem 10.6 and Lemma 10.7, pp. 43–48.

CM duality patches finite-level pairings through the same map and ultrafilter; perfectness of the dual system and augmentation compatibility are explicit hypotheses. Source: IKM24, 11.1–11.2 and Theorem 11.3, pp. 49–51.

Complex dimension uses the degree-shifted supremum over cohomology support and excludes the zero complex from finite numerical bounds. Source: CI21, Equations (1)–(4), Theorem 1 and Corollary 2, pp. 2–3.

The CM-base dual dimension identity has the correct depth/shift convention; it applies CI21 to the CM base rather than replanning a general big-CM existence theorem. Source: CI21, Proposition 6 and proof, p. 5; IKM24 Lemma 10.7, p. 48.

Codimension bounded by projective amplitude requires a nonzero finite perfect complex; equality forces top CM concentration under the stated dimension hypotheses. Source: IKM24, Lemma 10.7, p. 48; CG18 Lemma 6.2 and proof, pp. 385–386.

Derived length is a bounded finite-cohomology Euler invariant for a genuine finite action; its GrothendieckEulerForms input and base ring are explicit. Source: ACC23, §6.3.1–Lemma 6.3.4, published pp. 1048–1050.

The one-dimensional specialization identity uses the two-term parameter complex and torsion-free quotient lengths; higher Tor is retained in Euler form. Source: ACC23, Lemmas 6.3.2 and 6.3.4, published pp. 1047–1050.

Paired support transport uses the common mod-π action, genuine nonzero component data and dimension hypotheses; this algebraic target does not purport to prove an arithmetic Ihara lemma. Source: ACC23, §6.3.5, Assumption 6.3.6, Proposition 6.3.8, published pp. 1050–1052.

Nonzero support survives derived specialization at the stated local/parameter point by derived Nakayama; an ordinary quotient of one cohomology module is not the same assertion. Source: ACC23, Corollary 6.3.9 and proof, published pp. 1052–1053.

The finite characteristic-zero point argument is in KWII’s proof of Proposition 2.2(i), p. 9; the nonexistent Lemma 2.5 citation was replaced. Source: KWII, Proof of Proposition 2.2(i), p. 9 (finite one-dimensional quotient and its normalized valuation ring).

Full support over a reduced source and a surjective compatible ring map force a zero kernel; a nilpotent kernel over a nonreduced source need not vanish. Source: Tho15, Lemma 1.10, PDF pp. 8–9; Kisin09 (3.3.4), printed pp. 1158–1159.

Derived Nakayama requires the finite/perfect or derived-complete setting stated; an unrestricted complex is not tested by ordinary H⁰ reduction. Source: Pilloni20, Propositions 2.2.1–2.2.2, author p. 9; Lemma 2.3.1 and Proposition 2.3.1, author p. 10.

Derived specialization computes Tor and only its top cohomology is an ordinary quotient; the two-term S/(x) example detects lost lower degrees. Source: ACC23, Corollary 6.3.9 proof, published p. 1053; IKM24 Theorem 10.6(2)–(3), pp. 43–47.

Finite perfect derived completion is the local comparison with the imported reflector and Noetherian completion theorem, not a second completion construction. Source: Bhatt18, Lemma 5.3, PDF pp. 9–10; KT17 Lemma 2.13, PDF pp. 11–12.

Finite locally free determinants are imported from AlgebraicVectorBundles L0C; alternating determinants of a finite free resolution give only the trivialization adapter. Source: SGA2, Exposé XI, Lemma 3.15, new-edition p. 106 (old p. 134); Theorem 3.13(i), pp. 105–106 (old pp. 133–134).
